lines.text: A small land of rivers and islands on Africa's west coast, which fought hard for its freedom and has struggled to keep the peace. This is Guinea-Bissau.
Portuguese ships reached this coast in the fourteen hundreds, and for five centuries it was Portuguese Guinea.
Inland, the Mandinka kingdom of Kaabu grew out of a province of the Mali Empire and ruled much of the land until 1867.
In 1687 the Portuguese built a fort at Bissau, the start of the capital.
Amilcar Cabral, an agronomist and thinker, would found the party that fought for freedom, and lead it against Portugal.
His half-brother, Luis Cabral, would become the country's first president.
Joao Bernardo Vieira, a soldier, would rule for most of three decades, and be killed in office in 2009.
In 1959 striking dock workers were shot at Pidjiguiti, and the independence movement turned to arms.
In 1963 the war against Portugal began, and it would last more than a decade.
Umaro Sissoco Embalo would one day become president, in 2020.
Cabral was assassinated in 1973, months before independence was declared. In 1974 Portugal recognised the new nation.
In 1996 the islands of the Bijagos were made a biosphere reserve, a haven of mangroves and wildlife.
Two years later the country fell into civil war, which lasted into 1999.
And in November 2025 soldiers seized power once more, the day before election results were due.
Guinea-Bissau won its freedom by war, and is still searching for a lasting peace.
